div.head: AGu 5
div.ab: ⁊ ealle we cwædon on ða dæge ðe mon ða aðas swor, þæt ne ðeowe ne freo ne moton in ðone here faran butan leafe, ne heora nan ðe ma to us. Gif ðonne gebyrige, þæt for neode heora hwylc wið ure bige habban wille oððe we wið heora mid yrfe ⁊ mid æhtum, ðæt is to ðafianne on ða wisan, þæt man gislas sylle friðe to wedde ⁊ to swutulunge, þæt man wite, ðæt man clæne bæc hæbbe.

⁊ ealle hig gecwædon ða man þa aðas swor, þæt naðor ne we on ðone hére faran buton leafe, ne heora nan ða ma to us, buton man trywan ⁊ betwynan gyslas sylle, friðe to wedde ⁊ to swutelunge, þæt man mid rihte fare, gyf þæt geneodige, þæt ure ænig to oðrum fǽce mid yrfe and mid æhtum.

Et omnes ediximus in illa die qua iuramenta facta sunt, ne seruus uel liber audeant in exercitum ire sine licentia, nec eorum aliquis ad nos. Si eueniat, quod pro necessitate aliquis illorum erga nos emptionem uelit habere uel nos cum ipsis de pecore uel pecunia, hoc tolerandum est eo modo (eatenus), ut fideiussores dent ad uadium pacis et ostensionem, ut sciatur, quod clene bec (v[l]ex id est mundam carnem) habeat.

⁊ ealle we cwædon on ðam dæge ðe mon ða aðas swor, þæt ne ðeowe ne freo ne moton in ðone here faran butan leafe, ne heora nan ðe ma to us. Gif ðonne gebyrige, þæt for neode heora hwylc wið ure bige habban wille oððe we wið heora mid yrfe ⁊ mid æhtum, ðæt is to ðafianne on ða wisan, þæt man gislas sylle friðe to wedde ⁊ to swutulunge, þæt man wite, ðæt man clæne bæc hæbbe.

Und wir (sie B2) alle bestimmten an dem Tage, da man die Eide schwor, dass weder Höriger noch Freier (wir B2) in das [Dänen]heer ohne Erlaubniss auswandern dürften, noch einer jener [Dänen] ebensowenig zu uns. Wenn es aber vorkommt, dass aus Nothwendigkeit einer von jenen zu uns hin Handel mit Vieh und mit Waaren haben will, oder wir zu jenen hin, das ist in der Weise zu gestatten, dass man [der Händler] Geiseln gebe, dem Frieden zum Pfande und zum Beweise, dass bekannt sei, dass jener reinen Rücken habe. (zu uns; ausser wenn man Treugelübde und dazwischen Geiseln stelle dem F. z. Pf. u. z. B., dass man gesetzmässig reise, wenn [nämlich] es nöthig wird, dass unser einer zu [jenen] anderen ziehe mit V. u. m. W. B2).

And we (they B2) all determined on the day when the oaths were sworn that neither bond nor free (we B2) might go over to the [Danish] army without permission, nor any of those [Danes] to us either. But if it happens that out of necessity one of those wishes to trade with us in livestock and in goods, or we with them, that is to be allowed on condition that [the trader] give hostages as a pledge of peace and as proof, so that it may be known that he has a clean back. (to us; unless pledges of good faith and hostages between are given as a pledge of peace and as proof that one travels lawfully, if [namely] it becomes necessary that one of us goes to the others with livestock and goods B2).

And we all declared, on the day when the oaths were sworn, that neither slaves nor freemen should be allowed to pass over to the Danish host without permission, any more than that any of them [should come over] to us. If, however, it happens that any of them, in order to satisfy their wants, wish to trade with us, or we [for the same reason wish to trade] with them, in cattle and in goods, it shall be allowed on condition that hostages are given as security for peaceful behaviour, and as evidence by which it may be known that no treachery is intended.

And we all agreed on the day when the oaths were sworn, that no slaves nor freemen might go without permission into the army of the Danes, any more than any of theirs to us. But if it happens that from necessity any one of them wishes to have traffic with us, or we with them, for cattle or goods, it is to be permitted on condition that hostages shall be given as a pledge of peace and as evidence so that one may know no fraud is intended.
div.note: literally, “that one has a clean back”

Ein Sklave bedurfte auch im Inland zur Veränderung des Wohnorts der Erlaubnis. Wenn er also hier beim Auswandern in den Nachbarstaat neben dem Freien erwähnt wird, so erschien das für B 2 vielleicht als blosse formelhafte Redensart (s. Wb: freo S. 81 Z. 6), die auch ohne Sinnesänderung fortbleiben dürfe. Gemeint ist aber das Entlaufen über die Grenze, wogegen sich auch der spätere Vertrag zwischen England und den Nordleuten wendet; s. Gl unfrei 5a. f

A slave needed permission to change his place of residence even within the country. If, then, he is mentioned here alongside the freeman in connection with emigrating to the neighbouring state, this perhaps seemed to B 2 a mere formulaic phrase (see Wb: freo p. 81 l. 6) that could be left out without any change of sense. What is meant, however, is running away across the border, against which the later treaty between England and the Northmen is also directed; see Gl unfrei 5a. f
Ostangliens Volk unter Dänenherrschaft, ohne militärischen Sinn; Steenstrup Normannerne 276. Bessere daher Übs. nächster Zeile ‘[Dänen]’ in: [‘Ostanglier’]
The people of East Anglia under Danish rule, without any military sense; Steenstrup Normannerne 276. Accordingly, in the translation of the next line correct ‘[Dänen]’ to: [‘Ostanglier’]
S. Wb 225, Sp. 3, Z. 8 v. u.
See Wb 225, col. 3, l. 8 from the bottom.
for neade übersetzt Beda's necessitate cogente II 20. Doch passt auch ‘Geschäftsbedarf, -nutzen’; ‘business’ Earle
for neade translates Bede's necessitate cogente II 20. But ‘business need, business advantage’ also fits; ‘business’ Earle
wið m. gen. bezeichnet Richtung, Ziel; Toller s. v. I 1

Nicht ‘Kauf’ allein (Toller 1247b); laut letzter Zeile ist ‘Verkauf’ mitgemeint, wie gebycgean (s. Wb 4) ‘verkaufen’ heissen kann neben ‘kaufen’
Not ‘purchase’ alone (Toller 1247b); according to the last line ‘sale’ is meant as well, just as gebycgean (see Wb 4) can mean ‘sell’ as well as ‘buy’

Dies Bild zitieren Wbb. nur hierher. Toller (Suppl. s. v. bæc) hält richtig die Lesung in B 2 für blosse Formvariante. Sie beweist, zusammen mit Q (der zuerst die Wörter unübersetzt liess, dann missverstand), dass das Bild schon um 1100 ungebräuchlich war. Thorpe's Sinn ‘without deceit’ trifft zwar zu, erklärt aber das Bild nicht. Richtig scheint mir ‘Rücken (s. d. Gl) frei vom Tragen von Diebstahl’; Earle. Dass bæc von ‘Vergangenheit’ (Hodgkin) übertragen sein oder den ‘Rückhalt, Gewährsmann’ (Schmid) bedeuten könne, glaub ich nicht

Dictionaries cite this image only from this passage. Toller (Suppl. s. v. bæc) rightly regards the reading in B 2 as a mere variant of form. Together with Q (who at first left the words untranslated, then misunderstood them), it proves that the image had already gone out of use by about 1100. Thorpe's sense ‘without deceit’ is indeed correct, but does not explain the image. The right explanation seems to me to be ‘back (see that word in Gl) free from carrying theft’; Earle. I do not believe that bæc can be a figurative use for ‘the past’ (Hodgkin) or can mean ‘backing, warrantor’ (Schmid)
‘Fleisch’ Q Ld, unanfechtbare Viehware meinend. Diese Lesart flæsc stand neben bæc schon in lq, ist also zwar ebenso alt wie B, aber offenbar unecht
‘Flesh’ Q Ld, meaning livestock goods that cannot be challenged. This reading flæsc already stood alongside bæc in lq, and so is indeed as old as B, but is evidently not genuine
‘gegenseitig [ergänzt] sureties’ ungenau Price. Schmid will truwa ändern, mit Unrecht
‘mutual [supplied] sureties’ Price, inaccurately. Schmid would alter truwa, wrongly
Das Adverb übs. in medio, ad invicem; Toller
The adverb translates in medio, ad invicem; Toller
geneadian kennt Toller nur für ‘zwingen’; doch hat er neadian: ‘nötig sein’
Toller knows geneadian only in the sense ‘compel’; but he has neadian: ‘be necessary’

fæcc könnte Schreibweise von fecce sein, das aber ‘hole’ bedeutet, was nicht passt. Sweet Student's dict. 53 bietet, AGu 5 zitierend: ‘fæcan: deal [fācian]’ und facian: ‘try to get, aspire to’. [So Ælfred Oros. (ed. Sweet 152): Pirrus . . facade [erstrebte] Macedonia anweald für sperans Demetrium Macedoniā posse depelli.] Offenbar passt dieser Sinn hier nicht; auch müsste die Form facie lauten. Ich finde nichts Besseres als Price und Schmid's Emendation fare

fæcc could be a spelling of fecce, which, however, means ‘hole’, and that does not fit. Sweet Student's dict. 53, citing AGu 5, gives ‘fæcan: deal [fācian]’ and facian: ‘try to get, aspire to’. [Thus Ælfred Oros. (ed. Sweet 152): Pirrus . . facade [aspired to] Macedonia anweald for sperans Demetrium Macedoniā posse depelli.] Evidently this sense does not fit here; moreover the form would have to be facie. I can find nothing better than Price's and Schmid's emendation fare
Zu den zwei ersten Worten s. o. 2²·⁵.
On the first two words see above 2²·⁵.

In the 10th century the word here is frequently used (like O. Norse herr), without military significance; cf. IV Edg. cap. 15. It is not unlikely that here the expression in ðone here faran denotes simply a journey into Danish territory.
Lit. ‘that one has a clean back.’

Cap. 5 in B 2 reads as follows: ⁊ ealle hig gecwædon ða man þa aðas swor, þæt naðor ne we on ðone hère faran buton leafe, ne heora nan ða ma to us, buton man trywan ⁊ betwynan gyslas sylle, friðe to wedde ⁊ to swutelunge, þæt man mid rihte fare, gyf þæt geneodige, þæt ure ænig to oðrum fæce mid yrfe and mid æhtum.
